cues.text: A Boy Who Could Not Speak
At Easter 1461, Jehan Leclerc brought her twelve-year-old son Bertrand to Mass at the Church of St. Bartholomew in La Rochelle, France.
Bertrand had been paralyzed and mute since a serious fall five years earlier, at the age of seven, and had never fully recovered the use of his body or his voice.
When the time came for Communion, Bertrand indicated to his mother, as best he could without speech, that he too wished to receive the Eucharist.
The parish priest initially refused, since Bertrand's muteness made it impossible for him to make a sacramental confession beforehand.
But the boy persisted in his silent pleading until the priest, moved by his evident sincerity, relented and gave him Communion.
From the moment the Host touched his tongue, Bertrand felt himself seized by what witnesses described as a mysterious force, and within moments his paralysis lifted entirely and his voice returned.
According to the manuscript account compiled afterward, his very first words, spoken for the first time in five years, were drawn from Scripture: 'Our help is in the name of the Lord.'
A Church Already Marked by Relics

The healing took place in a church that already held its own relic of note — two drops of Christ's Blood, brought from the Holy Land in 1257 and preserved there for two centuries before Bertrand's cure.

The most authoritative surviving account of the 1461 healing is a painted manuscript still kept today in the Cathedral of La Rochelle, offering an unusually direct visual record of an event otherwise known only through later retelling.
The La Rochelle account belongs to a smaller category of Eucharistic tradition centered not on transforming the bread and wine.
Instead, it centers on healing granted at the moment of reception itself—the sacrament working, as the faithful understood it, exactly as it claimed to.
Whatever a modern reader makes of a five-century-old cure, the manuscript that recorded it, and the persistence of a mute boy together preserve a story.
He refused to be turned away from Communion, and his insistence was rewarded rather than fabricated for effect.
